questions.q: Why does the lesson say AI regressions are harder to notice than typical software regressions?
options: AI systems never actually regress in practice
AI regressions always crash the application immediately
An AI regression is quiet — the system still runs and returns a fluent, confident answer that's just subtly worse, with nothing visibly erroring
AI regressions only happen on weekends
questions.explain: The lesson explains that unlike a page erroring out, an AI regression produces a still-fluent but subtly worse answer with no visible crash.

questions.q: What are the four basic steps of the regression testing loop described in the lesson?
options: Guess, hope, ship, repeat
Delete the dataset, rebuild it, ignore results, repeat
Run the eval dataset as a baseline, make the change, run the same dataset again, and compare pass rates case by case
Train a new model, deploy it, wait for complaints, roll back
questions.explain: The lesson's basic loop is: baseline run, make the change, re-run the same dataset, then compare results case by case, not just in aggregate.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what makes a CI-integrated regression check more effective than a manually-run one?
options: CI checks are always more accurate than manual checks
It's wired into the same workflow as the code change itself, posting the before/after comparison right where the change is being reviewed
CI checks don't require an eval dataset at all
CI checks eliminate the need for human review entirely
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that automatic re-runs tied to the pull request workflow surface regressions where they'll actually be seen, rather than in a dashboard nobody checks.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a summary pass/fail count isn't enough on its own?
options: Because summary counts are always inaccurate
Because you still need to see what specifically changed in the output to judge whether the regression actually matters
Because CI tools cannot generate summary counts
Because summary counts take too long to compute
questions.explain: The lesson notes a count tells you that something regressed, but a human still needs to see the actual diff to judge whether it matters.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend doing with a newly discovered regression?
options: Ignoring it if it only affects one test case
Deleting the test case that revealed it
Adding it back into the eval dataset so the exact same mistake can never silently reappear
Waiting for a user to complain before taking any action
questions.explain: The lesson recommends feeding every newly discovered regression back into the eval dataset to prevent it from recurring unnoticed.
